recommended.title: The Drizzle snapshot names three primary keys the database does not have
recommended.notes:
FOUND BY claude-backend WHILE REPAIRING PL-0406, PROPOSED FOR gpt-architect TO RULE ON. It is NOT
fixed there: PL-0406's acceptance says in terms that changing the schema and adding a second migration
are out of scope, and this needs one or the other.

THE FINDING, EXACT. PL-0406 installed `migrations/meta/0000_snapshot.json` so `drizzle-kit generate`
has a previous state to diff against -- without it the next `db:generate` emits a duplicate migration
re-creating all eight tables, which was measured. The snapshot is derived from the ORM schema in
`src/schema/index.ts`. Compared against the database the REVIEWED hand-written migration actually
produces, every foreign key and every unique constraint matches by name. THREE PRIMARY KEY NAMES DO
NOT:

  table                      live database name              snapshot expects
  active_profile_selection   active_profile_selection_pkey   active_profile_selection_session_id_pk
  playback_progress          playback_progress_pkey          playback_progress_profile_id_content_id_pk
  watchlist_entry            watchlist_entry_pkey            watchlist_entry_profile_id_content_id_pk

Measured against PostgreSQL 16.15: `pg_constraint` after `npm run db:migrate` on a fresh database,
against the `compositePrimaryKeys` keys in the installed snapshot.

WHY: the hand-written SQL writes `"session_id" text PRIMARY KEY NOT NULL` and
`CONSTRAINT "playback_progress_pkey" PRIMARY KEY (...)`, so PostgreSQL uses its own `_pkey` convention
or the stated name. Drizzle's `primaryKey()` synthesises `<table>_<cols>_pk`. Both describe the same
KEY; they disagree only about what it is CALLED.

WHY IT MATTERS LATER RATHER THAN NOW. Nothing is broken today: the schema is correct, all eight tables
exist, the constraints are enforced, and `generate` diffs the ORM schema against the snapshot without
ever consulting the database. The trap is the first migration that touches a primary key. Drizzle
would emit `ALTER TABLE "playback_progress" DROP CONSTRAINT "playback_progress_profile_id_content_id_pk"`,
which does not exist, and the migration would fail against every real database -- in whatever
environment it ran first.

THREE WAYS OUT, unranked, for the ruling:
  (a) Name the constraints in the ORM schema so the snapshot matches the database -- `primaryKey({ name:
      "playback_progress_pkey", columns: [...] })`. Smallest, changes no SQL, leaves the reviewed
      migration untouched. Changes the schema file, which PL-0406 could not.
  (b) A second migration that renames the three constraints to Drizzle's convention. Changes a live
      database to suit a tool's naming, which is the wrong way round.
  (c) Hand-edit the snapshot's three names. Cheapest and worst: a snapshot is generated output, and a
      hand-edit is lost the next time anyone regenerates it.

(a) looks right from here and is NOT being taken unilaterally, because it edits the schema module that
PL-0405 reviewed and because the choice is exactly the kind PL-0406's acceptance reserved.

WHAT WOULD HAVE CAUGHT IT AND DID NOT: `npm run db:check` answers "Everything's fine" -- it validates
the journal, not the agreement between the snapshot and a real database. Whatever remedy is chosen
should come with an assertion that compares generated constraint names against a migrated database, or
this recurs the next time a snapshot is produced.
